title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Food & Agriculture
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Check Point’s gateway VPN flaw is now being exploited against its small-business firewalls, and a separate management-server zero-day has been in use since July — both entered KEV on 22 September
items.content_text: Check Point disclosed on 22 September that attackers have exploited CVE-2026-85102 (CVSS 9.8) against its Spark small-business firewalls and Security Gateways since 12 September, using unvalidated VPN-negotiation certificate data to gain unauthenticated remote code execution on the gateway. Check Point shipped a fix on 9 September; the Dutch NCSC’s warning three days later that exploitation was imminent has now been confirmed. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. No victim count or attribution has been given. Spark is Check Point’s small-business line, and that is where this lands in food and agriculture: co-operatives, packhouses, regional processors, and the depots and cold stores of larger groups typically run one small firewall — often managed by a service provider — as the only boundary protecting filling, packaging and refrigeration controls. No food or agriculture victim has been named.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Check Point security advisory of 22 Sep 2026 (sk1000117) and CISA’s 22 Sep 2026 KEV alert; the earlier Dutch NCSC warning as reported by BleepingComputer on 12 Sep 2026. No food-sector victims named

items.title: A China-linked actor emptied the code repositories of an industrial automation firm — SCADA and HMI tooling, not customer data
items.content_text: Acronis’s Threat Research Unit published research on 13 September on an actor it calls Red Heron, which has been exploiting a critical remote-code-execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code platform, CVE-2026-60004 (CVSS 9.8, fixed in Gitea 1.27.1 on 27 July); Acronis observed exploitation from 29 July to 4 August. The campaign scanned 1,386 self-hosted Gitea instances across seven countries and, per Acronis, produced 11 confirmed compromised targets in five countries — Canada, the United States, Taiwan, Argentina and Sri Lanka. The two that matter to industrial readers are a Taiwanese industrial automation company, from which hundreds of repositories were pulled, including a SCADA/HMI tool, IoT platform integrations and a network sniffer, and a Canadian renewable-energy operator, where Acronis counted 22 exploitation sessions, internal infrastructure mapping, three SSH key entries planted for persistence and 61 database dumps. The actor installed a custom C++ Linux implant the researchers call JITTERLY, with more than thirty post-exploitation commands, and an embedded LD_PRELOAD rootkit, SIXZUT. Attribution to a Chinese-speaking group is moderate confidence, based on language artefacts and tradecraft, and Acronis does not tie it to a known APT group; the apparent aim is espionage and source-code theft, not ransomware. No food or agriculture victim is named. The reason it belongs on this page is the target class: a food plant’s process knowledge does not only live in the plant. It lives in the machine builder’s and integrator’s repositories — PLC and HMI projects, recipe and batch logic, refrigeration control code, and the credentials commissioning engineers left in them.

items.title: Two small Colorado water utilities had PLC settings, alarms and pumping cycles altered by an unidentified foreign actor
items.content_text: SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber reported in detail on 21 and 22 September on a disclosure that first surfaced on 18 September: two privately owned Colorado water utilities, each serving fewer than 200 people, had their operational technology altered by an unidentified foreign actor in late August. The state’s account, given to Axios, is specific about what happened: attackers changed programmable-logic-controller settings, disabled the remote access an on-call operator relied on, disabled alarms, and altered pumping cycles. The disruptions were brief and did not affect water quality, treatment or public safety, and neither utility is named. Colorado’s governor’s office said only that it is aware of “ongoing efforts across the nation by an Iranian-backed group” to access drinking-water and wastewater systems, and explicitly could not confirm that group’s involvement in these two incidents; no CISA or WaterISAC advisory naming the event has been published, and no CVE applies. This is a water-sector story, and no food or agriculture victim is implicated. It earns a place here because the access path is not sector-specific: a small internet-facing PLC or HMI reached through a remote-access connection meant for an on-call operator is exactly what many single-site cold stores, packhouses and processing plants also run, typically with the same absence of a broker gateway or MFA that let this intrusion happen.
tags: Incident — Confirmed OT manipulation at two small utilities, attribution unconfirmed, cross-sector relevance

items.title: Ransomware against food and agriculture is up 62%, and the groups doing it schedule around harvest — now three weeks in
items.content_text: Food and Ag-ISAC figures, reported by Industrial Cyber on 3 and 8 September, put ransomware against food and agriculture at 227 incidents through July 2026 — a 62% rise on the 140 recorded in the same period of 2025, and enough to rank it the eighth most-targeted sector — and at 247 by the end of August. Qilin has been the most active group against the sector this year, with 47 listed attacks; Qilin, Akira, CL0P, Play and Lynx led in 2025. In a passage on Iranian activity against food security, the ISAC also states that federal agencies have confirmed attacks on internet-exposed programmable logic controllers used in processing lines and grain-handling systems. The finding that should change planning is the timing one. The FBI, as cited in the 8 September analysis, warns that criminals target food and agricultural cooperatives during planting (April–June) and harvest, and the September–November harvest window — when elevators, processing plants and cold-chain operators run at maximum throughput with the least tolerance for downtime — opened during this reporting period. The consequence argument is the other half, and it is the part that separates this sector from the rest of manufacturing. Loss of cold-chain and refrigeration telemetry forces product disposal regardless of whether the product was ever actually out of temperature, because compliance cannot be demonstrated without a continuous record. Compromise of production, quality or traceability data is treated by regulators as a food-safety event that triggers holds or recalls, not as an IT outage. This is analysis and sector data, not a report of a specific compromise; re-checked on 24 September, no named food or agriculture operator has reported an OT-disruptive incident since. What has changed is corroboration rather than impact: Black Kite’s 17 September report counts 1,183 ransomware victims across manufacturing and distribution in the first seven months of the year, and on 18 September Rockwell Automation extended its recovery guidance for controllers whose passwords were set by intruders to the Micro820 and Micro850 — the small PLCs that run packaging machines and utility skids in this sector. Leak-site claims against two agricultural-equipment makers surfaced on 18 September without any company statement and are not carried here.

items.title: Only 13% of network segments that contain OT devices hold OT alone — Forescout’s count of 47,700 segments
items.content_text: Forescout Vedere Labs published an analysis on 22 September of 47,700 network segments containing more than 2.5 million devices at 209 organisations. Its headline finding is that only 13% of segments containing OT devices are OT-only. Nearly half mix OT with IT and IoT assets, which widens the attack surface each OT device sits in. The average segment holds 54 devices of four device types. Business services, healthcare and oil and gas show the largest average “blast radius”. Forescout gives no figure for food, beverage, agriculture or manufacturing, so none is claimed here. The finding still describes a typical food plant closely. Line PLCs and HMIs often share a network with label printers, CCTV, badge readers, refrigeration and building-management controllers, the weighbridge PC and the QA lab. Plants that grew line by line and acquired sites that were never re-architected are the norm, not the exception. This is exposure research, not an incident report.

items.title: A North Korea-linked implant lived inside HAProxy load balancers, in front of every application and outside EDR’s view
items.content_text: Rapid7 Labs published research on 16 September on a previously undocumented Linux backdoor it calls TED, together with a tool named curlRAT, found embedded in HAProxy load balancers at a South Korean media organisation and a South Korean automotive company. Rapid7 attributes the activity with medium confidence to a North Korean state-aligned group adjacent to APT37. The implant sits where TLS terminates, in front of all the applications behind the load balancer, and Rapid7 describes it as generating no anomalous processes, no unexpected outbound connections and no log entries — it works by intercepting traffic that is already passing through, on a class of appliance that typically carries no endpoint detection agent. The purpose is espionage and interception; no production or operational-technology impact is reported and no food or agriculture victim is named. It is on this page because the same architecture exists at most multi-site processors: a reverse proxy or load balancer in the industrial DMZ fronting the historian portal, the MES web tier, vendor remote-access landing pages and cold-chain dashboards, built once by the network team and never put in the EDR estate. The point is the blind spot, not the attribution.

items.title: Ransomware against manufacturers is up 40% this year, and the growth has moved to Europe
items.content_text: Black Kite’s 2026 Manufacturing and Distribution Ransomware Report, covered on 17 September, counts 1,183 new ransomware incidents against manufacturers in the first seven months of 2026 — a 40% rise on the same period in 2025, and part of 5,237 disclosed victims across manufacturing and distribution since January 2023. The geography has shifted: the United States accounts for 412 attacks, still the largest single share at 35% but down from 52%, while Europe rose 85% to 369 (Germany 77, Italy 57, the UK 43, France 40) and the rest of the world nearly doubled to 402. Qilin leads the actor table, followed by The Gentlemen — a group with 142 claimed manufacturing victims by mid-2026, about 12% of the year’s total — then Akira, DragonForce and INC Ransom. About half of this year’s attacks came from groups that did not exist two years ago. Distribution logged 95 incidents in the first half of 2026 against 196 for the whole of 2025. Two caveats matter before anyone quotes this at a board. These are leak-site and disclosure counts, which measure claimed victims rather than confirmed OT-disruptive incidents. And the report covers manufacturing and distribution as a whole: food and beverage production sits inside that population, but the coverage gives no food-specific figures, so treat the trend as directional for this sector rather than as a sector count.

items.title: August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
items.content_text: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Food and beverage processors sit inside the manufacturing and business-services categories behind this record. The sector's own history — production stoppages that begin as IT events — is exactly the pattern the numbers describe.

items.title: Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
items.content_text: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. For food and beverage the consequence is a safety one, not just a production one: a compromised control system that produces an out-of-spec batch or a cold-chain excursion becomes a public-health problem. The argument is that engineered limits — mechanical stops, independent temperature cut-outs, physical verification steps — do more than any detection tool. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure.

items.title: Food and Ag-ISAC: confirmed attacks on exposed plant-floor PLCs, and a “shadow OT” estate nobody has counted
items.content_text: The Food and Ag-ISAC published its State of the Threat report on 3 September, and the operational findings matter more than the totals. Federal agencies have confirmed attacks on internet-exposed programmable logic controllers running processing lines and grain-handling equipment; hacktivist crews such as Dark Engine have demonstrated they can reach HMIs controlling automated machinery, irrigation and temperature-controlled storage; and the ISAC warns that “shadow OT” — networked silo sensors, automated feeders and cold-chain thermometers added for efficiency and never inventoried — is growing faster than most teams can track it. On volume, ransomware against food and agriculture reached 227 incidents through July, up 62% year on year, with Qilin (47), The Gentlemen (31) and Akira (14) the most active groups, making this the eighth most-targeted sector.

items.title: KEV’s 22 September batch is all edge and management plane: the SD-WAN orchestrator that configures every branch, an F5 access gateway and two Check Point flaws
items.content_text: CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 22 September, all with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. The two Check Point flaws are covered in the top story and the Check Point management card. The other two are infrastructure that food groups run more often than they realise. Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator, CVE-2026-93952, rated CVSS 10.0 in Arista Security Advisory 0183, is an improper-input-validation flaw in the on-premises orchestrator. Arista says it is known to be actively exploited. It is exposed when certificate-based Edge-to-Orchestrator authentication is configured, and no orchestrator credentials are needed. The hosted service is already patched; fixed on-premises builds are listed per release train in the advisory, and not every train had a fix at publication. Arista published indicators: the files .vcnode.js and vc-sysmond, the HTTP header x-vc-opt, and source addresses 142.93.149.77 and 104.248.126.159. F5 BIG-IP APM, CVE-2026-94127, rated CVSS 9.8, is a heap overflow giving unauthenticated code execution. It applies only where a virtual server carries both an APM access policy and an OAuth authorization-server profile. F5 has confirmed exploitation and issued engineering hotfixes under K000162605, and Rapid7 reports no confirmed public proof-of-concept. The orchestrator is the one to think hardest about. Multi-site food businesses — retail and foodservice distribution, processors with many depots, grocery chains — use SD-WAN to connect plants, DCs and branches. The orchestrator pushes configuration to every edge it manages, so a compromised orchestrator is a change at every site at once. No food or agriculture victim has been named for any of the four.

items.title: CISA’s 22 September batch: nine advisories, and the one most likely to reach a food line is inside other vendors’ firmware — the lwIP network stack
items.content_text: CISA published nine ICS advisories on 22 September, ICSA-26-265-01 to -09. The two that matter most on a food page are the first two, and neither is a product you buy directly. Both cover lwIP, the open-source lightweight TCP/IP stack embedded in a very wide range of microcontroller-based devices. ICSA-26-265-01 is an out-of-bounds write in lwIP’s MQTT client application, credited to Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay; public CVE records list it as CVE-2026-87121 at CVSS 9.8. ICSA-26-265-02 is a double free, credited to Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security. Which devices are affected depends on which vendors built lwIP’s MQTT client into their firmware, and that list does not exist yet. For this sector, MQTT is the protocol used by wireless temperature and humidity sensors, cold-store and reefer monitors, energy sub-meters and the IIoT gateways that feed line data to OEE and quality dashboards. The other seven advisories cover six Siemens products and one open-source runtime. For Siemens they are: Siveillance Control (unrestricted file upload), SIPLUS and SIMATIC products affected by the third-party “Copy Fail” Linux flaw, the Desigo CC building-management family (code injection, reported by Michelin CERT), Industrial Edge Management (a weak password-recovery mechanism in a third-party component), SIMOVE Fleetmanager and SIPLANT (path traversal), and WTV676 and WTV776 (improper input validation). The seventh is the end-of-life OpenPLC Runtime v3 (cross-site scripting). Industrial Edge Management is CISA’s republication of a Siemens item from the 8 September wave carried in the patch-wave card below. None of the nine is reported exploited or listed in KEV.

items.title: The remote-service VPN client machine builders use to reach Lenze x500 gateways runs injected commands as root — CVSS 9.6, fixed in 1.4.7
items.content_text: CERT@VDE published advisory VDE-2026-089 on 21 September for CVE-2026-75925 in the Lenze VPN Client, used with the Lenze x500 IoT Gateway, in versions 1.0.0 to 1.4.6. The advisory describes a CRLF injection (CWE-93). Configuration values the local service accepts are written to a file that a privileged subprocess later reads, and line-ending sequences are not neutralised. An attacker can therefore inject extra directives that run with root or SYSTEM privileges. The configuration interface does not check authentication, and injected settings survive restarts without any visible change in behaviour. The score is CVSS 3.1 9.6 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H). User interaction is required, which in practice means the engineer running the client. The fix is version 1.4.7, and the cloud service already refuses older clients with the message “A newer version of the VPN client is required”. The advisory documents no exploitation. The client is where this lands in food and beverage. Lenze drives and automation run on packaging, conveying and processing machinery, and machine builders use the x500 gateway and this client to service those lines remotely. The client therefore sits on an OEM service engineer’s laptop, or on your own maintenance laptop, and a compromised copy there is a persistent, privileged foothold on a machine that connects into your lines.

items.title: A small-site managed switch joins KEV — 996 Zyxel GS1900 units already had their configurations and root hashes pulled
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. The flaw is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN — or wherever the management interface is reachable — run operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel fixed it in June, in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and the per-model equivalents, and its advisory carries no CVSS score. What moved it into KEV is GreyNoise’s 21 September report on a single actor, active since 7 May and assessed as a Chinese speaker, that exploited 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries — Italy, the United States, Taiwan, France, South Korea and the Netherlands lead the count — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP; 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. The same actor stole records from a Western government organisation through two WordPress flaws and probed a long list of other products including Gitea, UniFi OS and Proxmox. GreyNoise infers an overlap with the Red Heron actor carried in the incidents section, and infers AI-assisted tooling from the iteration pattern; both are inferences rather than observations, and the cross-links to Zyxel’s own advisory and the KEV entry are the parts to rely on. The GS1900 is a small-office switch, which in this sector means the packhouse office, the depot, the farm shop, the weighbridge cabin and the cold store an acquisition brought with it. A switch whose configuration and administrator hash have been exfiltrated is not a patch problem; it is a rebuild-and-rotate problem.

items.title: A CVSS 10 bypass in Cisco ISE — the box that decides which devices are allowed onto the plant network
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, an authentication bypass rated CVSS 10.0 in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker reach the web-based management interface, and Cisco states its PSIRT “is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability”. All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — the interim control is infrastructure access lists restricting management traffic. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September, a three-day window that has now passed. No attacker attribution has been published, and no critical-infrastructure or industrial targeting is claimed; Singapore’s CSA issued its own alert on 21 September, and Cisco’s advisory remains at revision 1.0. Cisco’s hunting guidance is specific: search the ISE API gateway access log for the string “dummyuser”, and review the same log inside any support bundle. The reason it sits on a food and beverage page is what ISE usually does in these estates: it is the network access control and 802.1X policy engine that decides which laptops, contractor devices and plant machines are admitted to which VLAN, and it frequently underwrites the remote-access authorisation at the industrial DMZ. An attacker with administrative control of that policy engine does not need a plant exploit to reach the line.

items.title: Seven new CISA ICS advisories and one update on 17 September, and the PLC engineering software is the one to read first
items.content_text: CISA released seven new industrial control system advisories on 17 September, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update: Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. Mitsubishi’s CVE-2026-15688 is an authentication algorithm flaw in GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings rated CVSS v3.1 8.8 and v4.0 8.7, affecting all versions. The Modicon M340 advisory (-04) is CISA’s republication of a 2025 Schneider advisory: CVE-2025-6625, a crafted FTP command that can cause a denial of service, rated v3.1 7.5 and v4 8.7, fixed in M340 firmware SV3.70 with separate fixed versions for the Ethernet communication modules. NetBotz 5 (-05) carries CVE-2026-13336, an OS command injection rated v3.1 6.4 and v4 7.3, and CVE-2026-13337, a SQL injection, both fixed in 5.6.0. ABB Ability Edgenius (-06) is exposed to CVE-2026-31431, the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel privilege escalation rated v3.1 7.8, fixed in 3.2.4.1. PowerChute Serial Shutdown (-07) has CVE-2026-13348, an excessive-authentication-attempts weakness rated v3.1 5.3 and v4 6.9; Schneider’s remediation is version 1.6. The Bransys ELD advisory covers three hardcoded or cleartext credential issues in an electronic logging device for commercial trucking, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA reports no exploitation for anything in the batch. Separately, CISA updated ICSA-26-211-07 (Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN) on 17 September to add eight affected products. The Hitachi Energy advisory (-03) had not reached the public CSAF mirror at the time of writing, so its detail is not quoted here. For food and beverage readers the relevant pair is editorial rather than official: Modicon M340 is a common process and discrete controller on plant lines, and GX Works3 is the engineering software used to write and load Mitsubishi PLC logic — an authentication weakness there is a control-program integrity question, not only a workstation one.

items.title: One firmware, three vendors: CVSS 9.8 flaws in the IO-Link masters that sit on packaging and process lines
items.content_text: CERT@VDE published three coordinated advisories on 16 September for IO-Link master devices built on a common firmware older than 1.7.4: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 EIP DI8 and IOL MA8 PN DI8 (VDE-2026-027), Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2 and ICE3 modules (VDE-2026-014) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 devices (VDE-2026-028), all three carrying the same set of about 20 CVEs (CVE-2026-27546 to CVE-2026-27565). The two worst are rated CVSS 9.8: CVE-2026-27546, an unauthenticated bypass that grants administrator access, and CVE-2026-27565, which lets an unauthenticated attacker upload a malicious IODD device-description file that runs a shell script as root. Many further command-injection flaws score 8.8, and the set also exposes password hashes and SSH private keys. Phoenix Contact’s advisory credits Nozomi Networks. No exploitation is reported, and fixed firmware 1.7.8 is available. IO-Link masters are the gateways between the plant network and the sensors and actuators on automated equipment, which in a food or beverage plant often means filling, packaging, palletising and conveying machinery delivered by a machine builder. That is why the practical question is less “do we own these?” than “did our OEMs build them in?”.

items.title: Rockwell extends its “password you never set” recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the small PLCs on packaging machines and utility skids
items.content_text: Rockwell Automation revised its notice SD1790, Important Hardening Guidance and Instructions for Restoring Access When the Password Is Unknown, to revision 5.0 on 18 September, extending the hardening and recovery instructions originally written for MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers to the Micro820 and Micro850. The notice exists because of the FBI public service announcement of 30 July, which described attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none had existed, locking operators out of their own controllers. There is no CVE: the guidance is to remove controllers from direct internet exposure, reach them only through a VPN behind a firewall, set strong passwords, keep offline backups of the project files, disable the controller’s HTTP server where it is not needed, and stay on current firmware. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data; it widens the population the recovery procedure is written for. The food-sector relevance is editorial but direct. The Micro800 family is the low-cost controller a machine builder fits to a case packer, a checkweigher, a CIP skid or a small refrigeration plant, often with the builder’s remote-access modem beside it, and it is precisely the class of device the Food and Ag-ISAC described when it said federal agencies had confirmed attacks on internet-exposed PLCs in processing lines and grain handling. Recovering a locked controller during a run means a stopped line and, in a cold-chain application, a product-disposition decision.
tags: Advisory — Vendor hardening and recovery guidance, fifth revision, no CVE

items.title: ABB posts two advisories in two days: a missing length check in the Freelance DCS and a critical credential-reset flaw in dynovaPRO
items.content_text: ABB’s cybersecurity alerts page carries two new critical items dated in this window. On 18 September ABB published advisory 7PAA010706, Freelance — Missing Length Check, whose CSAF record identifies CVE-2023-5778 at CVSS v3.1 7.5; on 17 September it published 4JDE002044, dynovaPRO — Reset Credentials Vulnerability, rated CVSS 9.1 on ABB’s alerts listing. ABB’s listing page does not show CVE identifiers, affected versions or fixed releases, so nothing beyond the CSAF record is quoted here; read the PDFs before scheduling. Neither advisory reports exploitation, and no CISA republication was visible at generation time. Freelance is ABB’s compact distributed control system for process plants; where it appears in this sector it is typically the batching, utilities or CIP control layer at a dairy, brewery, sugar or edible-oil site rather than a packaging line. ABB’s listing gives no attack-vector detail, so treat reachability as unknown until the PDF is read; the dynovaPRO score is why the pair ranks above the routine advisory noise. dynovaPRO is a much narrower product, but a reset-credentials flaw in anything that fronts a control system deserves the same question: can an outsider reach the login page at all. The same ABB page also lists two 9 and 10 September advisories for the AC 800PEC family and Ability zenon relating to the Wibu CodeMeter licensing component, both rated 8.6.
tags: Advisory — Vendor PSIRT, dynovaPRO at CVSS 9.1, Freelance at 7.5, no reported exploitation

items.title: Three Linux kernel flaws entered KEV on 18 September — the kernel is inside the HMIs, edge gateways and IO-Link masters as well as the servers
items.content_text: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 18 September, across two alerts, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 September that has now passed: CVE-2025-39964, a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto interface; CVE-2026-53266, an out-of-bounds write in ebtables SNAT handling; and CVE-2025-39682, a flaw in kernel TLS zero-length record handling. No source found for this edition names the actor, the campaign or how the flaws are being used, and published CVSS figures differ between vendors and commentators, so none is quoted here. CISA’s catalog notes carry two warnings worth repeating: the affected kernel may be end-of-life in the product where it is found, and the component may be embedded in other vendors’ products. That second note is the food-sector point. The ABB Edgenius advisory in the 17 September CISA batch was itself a Linux kernel bug republished under an OT product name, and the same kernel sits inside panel-PC HMIs, cellular gateways at remote sites, the IO-Link masters carried above, refrigeration supervisors and the historian server. A KEV listing for the kernel is therefore a question for every OT vendor, not for the Linux administrator alone. Separately, on 18 September a researcher published working local-root exploits for four other kernel flaws; those are proof-of-concept only, are not in KEV and are not the same three vulnerabilities.

items.title: Moxa TN-4500B: an unauthenticated write in the web login knocks the switch over — fix is firmware 2.1
items.content_text: Moxa published advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in TN-4500B series switches running firmware 2.0 and earlier. An out-of-bounds write in the handling of the username field on the web login page lets an unauthenticated attacker crash the device, rated CVSS v4 8.8 with high availability impact and no confidentiality or integrity impact; the fix is firmware 2.1. No exploitation is reported. The TN-4500B is a ruggedised switch built for rolling stock and vehicles, so it is uncommon in a food plant, and this card ranks Medium here for that reason. It stays on the page because Moxa managed switches in general are common in packaging halls, cold stores and outdoor agricultural installations, and the shape of the flaw — a login page that can be broken before any credential is checked — is the same test to run on every industrial switch with a web interface: can anything other than an engineering host reach it.

items.title: mySCADA myPRO Manager flaw rated CVSS 9.8 opens management functions and the SMS alarm modem
items.content_text: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03, released on 15 September, covers mySCADA myPRO Manager version 2.1 and earlier. CVE-2026-73807 is a missing-authorization flaw rated CVSS v3 9.8, and CVE-2026-82567 is a missing-authentication flaw in a critical function rated 6.3. According to CISA, they could let an attacker reach privileged management functions or send arbitrary SMS messages through a GSM modem connected to the system. CISA lists Food and Agriculture among the affected sectors, alongside critical manufacturing, energy, transportation and water. The fix is version 2.2, and CISA reports no known public exploitation. The SMS detail is the sector-relevant one: smaller processors, cold stores and agricultural sites often rely on text alerts for out-of-hours alarms, so a channel an outsider can write to is a channel staff may stop trusting.

items.title: September’s ICS patch wave lands in the process-control layer that also enforces food safety
items.content_text: Schneider Electric and Siemens both shipped critical fixes on 8 September. The most consequential for food and beverage plants is a critical authentication vulnerability in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2 — the safety variant is the part worth pausing on. Siemens published seven advisories the same day, spanning Reyrolle protection relays, Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager. Both arrive on top of the 3 September Inductive Automation Ignition flaw, CVE-2026-77393 at CVSS 8.8, which sits in the HMI and SCADA layer of a great many processing sites. None is reported exploited. What makes this a sector story rather than a patch list is the point Industrial Cyber made on 8 September: in food manufacturing, process control is food-safety control. Cook and pasteurisation setpoints, chemical dosing, cold-chain holds and batch integrity all live there.

items.title: GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and food and beverage teams host more of it than they think
items.content_text: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Food and beverage processors version recipe management, batch control integrations, MES and warehouse-management interfaces, and cold-chain telemetry code in self-hosted GitLab. Unauthenticated reads against that repository expose both the process knowledge and the service credentials that reach packaging lines and refrigeration control.

items.title: Nozomi’s second SCALANCE LPE9403 study: 12 flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September, bringing the total to 12 vulnerabilities — nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client, scored between CVSS 5.3 and 8.5. Firmware below V4.0 HF0 and Edge Client releases through V2.1 are affected, and Siemens has published an advisory and patches; V4.0 HF0 and later carry the fixes. The finding that matters is not any single score: Nozomi demonstrated that several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of OT services and lateral movement onto connected networks. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Two dates are worth keeping straight, because the coverage has muddled them. The first part of this research, published 10 September, described four PROFINET DCP denial-of-service flaws rated CVSS 5.3 (CVE-2025-40575 to CVE-2025-40578) in a daemon that runs as root without authentication on every device interface. The underlying CVEs were originally disclosed in May 2025 under CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18; what happened on 15 September was an update to that advisory adding the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and vendor fixes, not a new critical vulnerability. Processing and packaging lines that use the LPE9403 to aggregate PROFINET data for MES or cloud analytics should read the chained-root result as the reason to close the firmware gap rather than defer it.

items.title: A ransomware operator is picking encryption targets from inside Cisco firewall management — that is how a plant stops
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco patched it in early March and published indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to KEV with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos reports three clusters. UAT-12197, unattributed, exploited CVE-2026-20079 and deployed a web shell and malicious JAR to harvest credentials. UAT-11823, an APT cluster whose tooling overlaps with Sandworm’s, exploited both CVE-2026-20079 and the earlier CVE-2026-20316 and deployed a Cyclops Blink variant. UAT-11988, a ransomware operator, came in only through CVE-2026-20316 using static credentials, performed reconnaissance and compiled endpoint lists for encryption; Talos assesses with high confidence that its tactics are consistent with Qilin ransomware affiliates. On 16 September Cisco shipped the accompanying hardening release, advisory cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN: eight internally found CVEs, CVE-2026-20329 through CVE-2026-20336, up to CVSS 9.9, fixed across ASA, FTD and FMC. Food and beverage operators should read the Qilin detail literally. The sector’s production stoppages this year have followed that shape — enterprise intrusion, target enumeration, then encryption reaching the systems batching, packaging and refrigeration depend on. FMC is where the boundary meant to prevent that is configured.

items.title: The MikroTik router chain moved from disclosed to exploited — unauthenticated admin over SSH
items.content_text: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS flaws known as the “MikroTrick” chain, previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited, are now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication bypass, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed by ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. This is a change of exploitation status, not a new vulnerability. It is on this page for the same reason the Cisco item is: the box sitting between a remote site and everything else is usually the cheapest thing in the estate and the least likely to be on anyone’s asset register.

items.title: A second Check Point management-server flaw was a zero-day for two months — CVE-2026-93616 was used in targeted attacks on 23 July and fixed on 22 September
items.content_text: Check Point’s 22 September advisory disclosed CVE-2026-93616, rated CVSS 9.8. It is a pre-authentication path traversal in the Security Management web service that can lead to script execution and Java class loading on the server. Check Point says it observed a handful of pinpointed attacks using it on 23 July 2026, roughly two months before the fix it released on 22 September. CISA added it to KEV the same day, with a federal deadline of 25 September. As reported by Help Net Security and The Hacker News, the affected components are Security Management Server, Multi-Domain Security Management, Log Server, Multi-Domain Log Server and SmartEvent; the fix is published under sk1000171, and The Hacker News reports that end-of-support R81.10 and older builds are affected with no fix. Check Point has not named the targets or the actor. This is a different flaw from CVE-2026-91843, the over-long-username overflow in the next card, which remains unreported as exploited. What matters for a food or beverage group is what the server holds: one management server usually writes the policy for every gateway in the estate — plant, distribution centre, cold store and co-packer tunnel — so an intruder on it can change the boundary between the enterprise and production networks everywhere at once, without touching a single gateway.

items.title: A CVSS 9.8 flaw in Check Point’s management server hands root to an unauthenticated login request — the console that writes every plant’s firewall rules
items.content_text: Check Point has fixed CVE-2026-91843, rated CVSS 9.8, in its Security Management and Log Servers, as reported by The Hacker News on 17 September and in SecurityWeek’s round-up of 18 September. The flaw is a stack overflow in the login process: an unauthenticated request carrying an overly long username can lead to code execution as root. The Hacker News reports that a Trusted Clients misconfiguration is a precondition; that detail could not be confirmed in the vendor text, so treat it as reported rather than settled. Affected builds are R82.10 up to JHF Take 44, R82 up to Take 126, every R82.20 build (no protective jumbo hotfix yet), R81.20 up to Take 166, R81.10 up to Take 190, and the end-of-support R81 and R80.x lines. Multi-Domain Server is affected; Smart-1 Cloud is already fixed. Check Point says there is no indication of exploitation in the wild. This is a separate issue from the two VPN flaws in the top story, and from CVE-2026-93616, the management-server zero-day in the card above that was exploited from July; the reporting reviewed for the 24 September edition shows no exploitation of CVE-2026-91843 itself. In a food or beverage group, one management server usually holds the policy for every gateway — plant, distribution centre, leased cold store and co-packer tunnel — so whoever controls it can reshape the boundary between the enterprise and production networks without touching a gateway directly.

items.title: CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV — including the tool your line OEM dials in with at 3 am
items.content_text: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 10 and 11 September after evidence of active exploitation, reported together on 12 September, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS and 14 September for ScreenConnect (both passed) and 25 September for Artifactory, which arrived today. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to obtain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload. The RouterOS entry is the CERT Polska chain carried separately here. ScreenConnect is the one that matters most on a food page. Filling, labelling, palletising and refrigeration vendors support their equipment remotely, often out of hours during a run, and the agent that makes that possible is usually installed at commissioning on the same PC that programs the line.

items.title: The rest of the September patch wave: Siemens Reyrolle, Industrial Edge Management and hardcoded keys in Aveva
items.content_text: Beyond the Modicon and Ignition items, the 8 September wave carried several findings worth logging even where the equipment is not on a food line. Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 covers fourteen CVEs in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relays, all versions before V2.70; the lead flaw, CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS v3.1 9.8, lets an attacker derive current and past session identifiers from data the web interface leaks and bypass authentication. Weak session entropy and a role-based access control bypass granting administrator rights sit alongside it. Siemens issued nine advisories in total, also naming Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager, and began shipping fixes for Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431. Aveva disclosed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, including a hardcoded encryption key and MD5 password hashing; CISA formalised those on 10 September as advisory ICSA-26-253-01 — CVE-2026-81821 and CVE-2026-81822 both at CVSS v3 8.4, CVE-2026-81823 at 5.3 and CVE-2026-81824 at 4.7, affecting versions up to and including 2025_SP1_P1 and fixed in the 2025 SP1 P2 security update. It was the only new ICS advisory CISA published in the 9–11 September window. None is reported exploited.

items.title: CISA and the FBI on integrator risk: one compromised automation vendor, nine zip files, about 800 files of its customers’ SCADA details
items.content_text: CISA and the FBI published a joint fact sheet on 24 September, Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working with Third-Party ICS Integrators. It cites a case from March–April 2025 in which foreign cyber actors compromised a US industrial automation company that provided system integration and SCADA programming, and staged nine zip files holding roughly 800 files of customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics. The customers named are power utilities and transportation entities; food and agriculture is not mentioned, and the fact sheet does not name the integrator or the actor. Its recommendations are least-privilege access for every integrator, secured and monitored remote access, an inventory of the hardware and software each integrator supplied and how it connects, cybersecurity and supply-chain terms in contracts, minimal internet exposure, and offline backups with practised manual operation. The fit for food and beverage is direct: the machine builders and integrators who commission filling, packaging, retort, refrigeration and ammonia-plant controls usually hold the project files and often a standing remote-access path. The Red Heron theft of an automation firm’s SCADA and HMI repositories, carried above, is the same risk from the attacker’s side.

items.title: NIST’s draft rewrite of the OT security guide names food and agriculture in its scope for the first time — comments are due 30 November
items.content_text: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, on 21 September, with public comments due by 30 November 2026. According to NIST’s publication page, the revision expands the guide’s scope. It adds building automation and control systems, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and IIoT and cloud convergence. It also restructures the guidance around the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 and improves the sections on asset management, network monitoring and detection, and zero-trust principles. Industrial Cyber’s 22 September review of the draft notes its emphasis on consequence-driven risk management and on separating OT from enterprise networks. For a sector that has usually borrowed its OT security baseline from manufacturing or water, this is the first NIST OT guide to name food and agriculture explicitly. It is also the document auditors, insurers and large retail customers are most likely to cite next. It is a draft, not a requirement, and it imposes no obligation.

items.title: HKCERT: patching an edge device does not evict whoever is already on it — assume breach at the VPN, firewall and router layer
items.content_text: Hong Kong’s computer emergency response team published an advisory on 15 September, covered by Industrial Cyber on 21 September, warning that VPN appliances, firewalls, routers and remote-access systems remain the primary route into internal networks, and that patching alone does not remove stolen credentials or persistent access from a device that was already compromised. HKCERT recommends an assume-breach posture for internet-edge devices: multi-factor authentication on every remote path, credential rotation after patching rather than before, and monitoring for lateral movement from the edge into enterprise and operational networks. The advisory cites no specific incident. It is carried here as the summary line under the edge cards on this page — Cisco ISE and FMC, MikroTik, Zyxel GS1900, Check Point, the Linux-kernel trio — because the pattern across all of them is the same, and because the food sector’s edge is unusually thin: a single firewall or cellular router at a plant, a packhouse or a grain site is often the only boundary between the internet and the line.

items.title: CISA makes the case for decoys — a detection method you can add without touching the process
items.content_text: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The premise is unsentimental: assume an attacker will eventually obtain some access, and plant assets whose only purpose is to be touched by someone who should not be there. The guide covers tripwires, breadcrumbs and honeytokens, positions them alongside Zero Trust rather than instead of it, and structures the work in three phases — preparation, execution and analysis — to be iterated with red-team exercises. Planning is framed around the three MITRE Engage goals of expose, affect and elicit, with detections mapped to ATT&CK and deliberate attention to the living-off-the-land activity that signature-based tooling misses. Industrial Cyber’s coverage reports a detailed water and wastewater case study in the document, including decoys placed to look like OT HMIs; SecurityWeek’s write-up does not mention water or OT, so treat the OT case study as that outlet’s reporting until you have read the PDF. The reason this suits food and beverage plants is the one thing decoys do not require: a change to a live control system. A fake historian share, a false engineering-workstation credential or an HMI-looking host on the plant VLAN costs no production risk and no vendor sign-off.

items.title: CISA retires its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — check whether your process reads it
items.content_text: CISA is discontinuing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin with effect from 28 September 2026, reported on 17 September. The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, alerts and advisories all continue; the change is framed as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation set out in Binding Operational Directive 26-04 in June 2026. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected. For food and beverage operators the practical question is narrow and easy to check: does anything in your vulnerability-management routine, or in a managed service provider’s, consume that weekly bulletin as a feed or as the trigger for a review meeting? Small and mid-sized processors in particular tend to have one person who reads a weekly digest rather than a subscription to per-advisory feeds, and a source that stops arriving quietly is worse than one that stops loudly.

items.title: ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
items.content_text: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Food and beverage processors are beneficiaries rather than regulated parties, unless they place connected products on the EU market themselves. The practical gain is faster, more consistent vulnerability disclosure from the vendors of line control, packaging and cold-chain equipment. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate.

items.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting went live on 11 September — your line and refrigeration vendors now have 24 hours
items.content_text: The vulnerability and incident reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must now notify an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe security incident through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform within 24 hours of becoming aware, follow up within 72 hours with exploit and mitigation detail, and file a final report within 14 days of a fix becoming available, as well as informing affected users. It applies to manufacturers placing products on the EU market wherever they are based, with penalties up to €15 million. For a food or beverage processor this cuts two ways. Your filling, packaging, palletising, refrigeration and ag-IoT suppliers — many of them European — are now on a 24-hour clock, so you should hear about exploited flaws sooner. And if your group builds or badges any connected product sold into Europe, the obligation may apply to you directly.

items.title: 117 federal cyber incident reporting rules, and the argument that they pull staff off the response
items.content_text: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September counting, from GAO figures, 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than political: in the first hours of an incident, the people who understand the affected systems are the same people drafting duplicate notifications in different formats to different regulators on different clocks. The timing matters because CIRCIA’s implementing rules are expected to be finalised this autumn. A food or agriculture business feels this acutely if it also handles payment card data, holds regulated financial or health information, ships product to state agencies, or operates in the EU alongside NIS2 and Cyber Resilience Act duties — a single ransomware event at a processing site can trigger several clocks at once.
